newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tall ships to set sail in Hong Kong-Japan race.
newsitem.headline: Tall ships to set sail in Hong Kong-Japan race.

text.p: A century and a half ago, tall ships anchored off Hong Kong when the British sailed into China with opium and returned with silk, silver and tea.

This week, brigantines and schooners were back but the gunboat diplomacy of yesteryear lost in preparations for a 2,640 nautical mile race from Hong Kong to Osaka as part of the Japanese city's centennial celebration as a modern port.

With their masts and sails looking wonderfully out of place alongside container carriers, speedy ferries and rusting hulks plying Victoria Harbour, the ships from 18 countries and territories will sail out of Hong Kong on Friday.
Prizes will go to the winners but race director Kaoru Ogimi said he prefers to call the event a "festival of sail".
"They're not here to beat each other," Ogimi told Reuters. "They're here to promote international understanding and friendship."

The event has already been touched by tragedy. The Queen Charlotte, a New Zealand ship sailing to join the second leg off Japan, broke up in a tropical cyclone last week. The search for the five crew members was abandoned.
The armada ranges from Denmark's all-wood Jens Krogh built in 1899 to Russia's huge three-masted Pallada and its sister ship, the Dar Molodziezy from Poland.
Hong Kong's lone entry, the 40-metre (131-foot) Ji Fung, will lead the 10 tall ships and 20 yachts in a parade of sail on Friday morning before the month-long race starts in open water.
The number of ships will swell to more than 50 by the time the fleet reaches Osaka around April 27, organisers say.

"There's some great competition out there and I think everybody will be trying to win," said Greg Tonnison, captain of the Ji Fung. "But it's all about fun and different people and different countries getting along with each other."
Parties and receptions are planned at the ports of call along the way, he said, adding that the Russian and Italian ships brought along their own bands.

The first leg from Hong Kong to the southern Japanese island of Okinawa will be the most difficult, Tonnison said, because of the lingering northeast monsoon and other strong winds. "We've been to Japan three times at a similar time of the year and we've had a very mixed bag of weather," he said.

The event also faced problems getting going in Hong Kong. Organisers tinkered with the "Sail Osaka '97" name by adding "Hong Kong Tall Ships Spectacular" to boost local interest and staged a carnival weekend, public tours of the Ji Fung and a maritime history exhibition.
By hoisting the sails and leaning into the wind, the participants were taking a step back from the "faster, bigger, more" credo of modern society, Ogimi said.
Tonnison echoed Ogimi's enthusiasm. "It's going to be a great trip, especially seeing some of these big boys with all their sails set."
